record.reply: The imperfect duty of beneficence already binds Ada to try to save a life when she can. That duty does not change when the stated probabilities move; what shifts is how well each available act can realize that same duty. As long as both patients are strangers and neither has a special claim, the duty gives Ada latitude but also requires that the adopted maxim be capable of being a universal law. A maxim such as “When I must choose which of two strangers to treat, I will give the treatment where it has the higher chance of success” can be willed universally because it seeks the same end of aiding others while using available resources rationally. If the probabilities reversed, the same duty would direct the medicine to the now-better-off patient. Thus the comparative numbers do not create a new duty but guide the practical specification of the existing one.
record.framework_commitment: Kantian imperfect duty of beneficence requires adopting a maxim that pursues others’ welfare where one is able; effectiveness is a morally relevant specification of that maxim.
record.reasoning_bridge: 1. Duty: aid others when feasible (imperfect). 2. Both Ben and Cara qualify. 3. Imperfect duties allow choice of maxim. 4. A rational, universalizable maxim favors the action that more probably achieves the duty’s end. 5. Therefore give medicine to patient with 95 % chance. Probabilities matter to effectiveness, not existence, of duty.
record.remaining_uncertainty: Boundary where probabilities are roughly equal: fairness or randomization could then be an equally universalizable maxim. We do not know the exact threshold at which effectiveness difference becomes morally insignificant.
record.reversal_condition: If Ben’s chance were at least as high as Cara’s, the same reasoning would reverse the allocation.
